column4: The oath to the sun and its ضُحَىٰ names the same spreading morning light and gives the closest Quranic counterpart to 93:1.
The oath to night إِذَا يَغْشَىٰهَا stages night covering the sun, directly matching the section's cloth-like closure over light.
The oath to night إِذَا يَغْشَىٰ repeats the covering action, while this surah places that covering night before the revealed day of 92:2.
Day إِذَا تَجَلَّىٰ becomes manifest after the covering night of 92:1, reversing 93's light-first order and showing the cover lift.
God darkens the sky's night and brings out its ضُحَىٰ, making the section's morning light something drawn forth from darkness.
God makes night so people may تَسْكُنُوا۟ in it and day visible; the S-K-N verb is the very definition used in the source to hear stillness behind سَجَىٰ.
Night is made لِبَاسًۭا, the Quran's explicit realization of the section's image of cloth laid over the world.
One ayah makes night a garment, sleep repose, and day نُشُورًۭا; the covering is temporary and the covered sleeper rises again.
God wraps night over day and day over night, so each covering is laid on and removed by the reciprocal cosmic order.
Night and day are made خِلْفَةًۭ for remembrance or gratitude, stating the purpose that the section finds in their regular succession.
The identical prohibition وَلَا تَنْهَرْهُمَا uses نهر in the same sense, forbidding rebuke of parents as 93:10 forbids rebuke of the asker.
God cleaves daybreak, makes night سَكَنًۭا, and sets sun and moon for reckoning, joining emerging light, settled night, and measured time.
Night is made for rest and day مُبْصِرًا; the paired gifts reproduce the still cover and unobstructed visibility of the section.
God makes night for rest and day visible, then calls this divine bounty and notes how few give thanks, joining the image to the surah's thankful close.
Night for rest and day for seeking bounty are explicitly made from mercy so that people may give thanks, gathering the section's repose, provision, and gratitude.
The night sign is effaced and the day sign made مُبْصِرَةً so people seek bounty and count time; darkness and visible light remain purposeful paired signs.
God strips day from night, whereupon people are in darkness; this concrete removal makes light's disappearance a reversible covering action rather than a void.
The oath to night إِذَا عَسْعَسَ presents it withdrawing, a dynamic boundary to 93's settled night, and opens directly onto the breathing dawn of 81:18.
The oath to dawn إِذَا تَنَفَّسَ makes light breathe out after the retreating night, a close nonlexical parallel to the spread of ḍuḥā.
The oath to night إِذْ أَدْبَرَ shows the cover turning away, contrasting its motion with سَجَىٰ's stillness and leading into 74:34.
The oath to morning إِذَآ أَسْفَرَ stages brightness disclosed as night recedes, matching the lifting of the section's cover.
The oath to day إِذَا جَلَّىٰهَا says day displays the sun, spelling out the revealing spread implicit in ḍuḥā and completed by covering night in 91:4.
Night covers day in a rapid pursuit; the same covering scene also sharpens how unusual 93's motionless, lingering سَجَىٰ is.
God يُغْشِى ٱلَّيْلَ ٱلنَّهَارَ, another direct formulation of night laid over day as a covering.
God extends the shade, could have made it سَاكِنًۭا, and makes the sun its guide; moving light and potentially still cover meet in one measured scene.
God then draws the extended shade back gradually, completing 25:45's sun-guided scene and showing a cover removed by degrees.
God takes people by night and raises them again by day, so the nightly cessation preserves rather than abandons what will awaken.
Dark pieces of night are said to cover condemned faces; night becomes almost material cloth here, while its punitive use reverses the section's sheltering calm.
At sunrise a people have no سِتْرًۭا from the sun, a concrete scene of unobstructed light that also supplies the opposite boundary to night as cover.
The oath to night وَمَا وَسَقَ presents night gathering and enclosing what it contains, close to the section's world closed over and stilled.
The oath to night إِذَا يَسْرِ makes night travel away; that passing movement illuminates by contrast the persistence heard in سَجَىٰ.
The counterfactual of unending night asks who could bring light; it marks the boundary where a removable cover would become permanent and confirms that light's return is divine provision.
The counterfactual of unending day asks who could bring a night in which people rest, showing that unbroken brightness would also violate the merciful alternation.
Cloud above layered sea and waves produces darkness in which a hand is scarcely visible; this is the exact atmospheric reverse of the source's dictionary sense of cloudless, unobstructed light.
A storm from the sky contains darknesses, thunder, and lightning, supplying the clouded and unstable opposite of the source's clear bright day and continuing in 2:20.
Intermittent lightning lets people walk, while darkness makes them stand still; unstable flashes and enforced stillness contrast with steady ḍuḥā and settled, enduring night.
Piled cloud, hail, and nearly blinding lightning place brilliant light inside cloud itself, a specific boundary to the dictionary image of light with no cloud intervening.
Paradise promises that one will not تَضْحَىٰ, suffer exposure to the sun; this verbal branch of ض ح و marks the bodily limit of the section's welcomed morning brightness.
Night's rising is described as firmer in impact and straighter for speech; it turns the time made for repose into wakeful recitation while retaining its special stillness.
Sleep is made سُبَاتًۭا, the repose that the next ayah's night-garment shelters and that 25:47 also joins to night.
Day is made مَعَاشًۭا after the night-garment of 78:10, giving the lifted cover its active, life-sustaining consequence.
Whatever سَكَنَ in night and day belongs to God; its S-K-N wording echoes the source's definition of سَجَىٰ and places all settled things within both times.
The same temporal noun ضُحًۭى marks the forenoon when punishment might arrive as people play, showing that the bright hour does not by itself guarantee safety.
Moses fixes the public gathering for ضُحًۭى on the festival day, using the source word in its straightforward sense as a named, fully visible hour.
Resurrection makes worldly duration seem only an evening or its ضُحَىٰ; the named morning hour becomes a measure of how quickly an apparently lasting interval passes.
God inserts night into day and day into night, a direct account of the cover and light entering one another rather than either being lost.
God's insertion of night into day and day into night presents their changing lengths as deliberate action under the One who hears and sees.
Night enters day and day enters night while sun and moon run to fixed terms, joining extension of the two times to measured celestial order.
Night and day enter one another as sun and moon run to appointed terms, another formulation of the regular, removable covering central to the section.
God inserts night into day and day into night and knows what hearts contain; cosmic covering therefore never implies divine absence or ignorance.
God alternates night and day and calls that alternation a lesson for people of sight, closely matching the section's reflective use of the two times.
The alternation of night and day is a sign for the mindful, so their repeated exchange carries meaning rather than marking abandonment.
The alternation of night and day stands among signs for people of understanding, supporting the section's reading of their order as intelligible address.
The alternation of night and day is included among concrete created signs for those who reason, giving the image its wider cosmic setting.
Life, death, and the alternation of night and day are placed together under God's agency, making each cessation part of a governed return.
Night-day alternation is joined to life-giving provision from heaven and called a sign for those who reason, linking the cycle to provision rather than withdrawal.
God creates night, day, sun, and moon, each moving in an orbit; the two states belong to a continuous ordered motion.
Night cannot outstrip day and every luminary moves in an orbit, setting a firm boundary around their reliable succession.
Sun and moon are subjected دَآئِبَيْنِ and night and day are subjected for people, making persistence and regular service features of the same cycle.
Night, day, sun, and moon are all subjected by God's command and offered as signs, grounding both illumination and cover in one governance.
Night and day, along with sun and moon, are God's signs; the ayah directs worship past the visible times to their Creator.
God measures night and day while humans cannot keep exact account, a direct counterpart to the section's attention to rising, extension, and named degrees of daylight.
Day brings سَبْحًۭا طَوِيلًۭا, prolonged movement or occupation, which complements 73:6 and contrasts with the settled world heard in سَجَىٰ.
Sleep by night and day and seeking God's bounty are paired signs, widening repose beyond darkness while keeping rest and provision in the daily order.
God takes souls in death and sleep, retains some and releases others; it makes sleep a temporary holding whose release clarifies how covering need not be loss.
Twilight is sworn by immediately before the gathering night of 84:17, preserving the visible threshold at which spreading day becomes cover.
The full moon is sworn by after the gathering night, giving a concrete Quranic instance for the source dictionary's secondary sense of a night bright like ḍuḥā.
The oath by dawn names the first breach of night, an earlier boundary of the same morning light that rises and spreads into ḍuḥā.
Calling God the Lord of ٱلْفَلَقِ presents daybreak itself as a divinely opened breach through darkness.
The night of 97:1 remains peace until the rising of dawn, so settled night has a stated boundary and ends without ceasing to be a gift.
Lot is told to travel in the night and that the appointed morning is near; the dark interval carries divine care toward an assured morning.
The descending messengers speak only by the Lord's command and say that the Lord is not forgetful, a direct parallel to speech entering an apparent silence to deny abandonment.
Clothing is said to cover nakedness and provide adornment, supplying the concrete covering function that makes night as لِبَاس intelligible.
Even when people cover themselves with garments, God knows what they hide and disclose; a cloth cover therefore cannot entail divine absence or lost knowledge.
The sun is made radiance and the moon light, with phases for counting years; it joins bright day, luminous night, and time's measure in one ordered scene.
God places a lamp and an illuminating moon in the sky, furnishing a concrete nocturnal light for the source dictionary's bright-night sense.
The moon is made a light and the sun a lamp, pairing nocturnal illumination with the source of spreading daylight.
The moon is sworn by just before the retreating night and brightening morning, contributing nocturnal light to that three-part transition.
Sun and moon move by precise calculation, supporting the section's treatment of bright times and their extension as measured rather than accidental.
God creates the darknesses and the light; their darkness-first order provides a broad cosmic reversal of 93's light-first opening.
At the cave, the rising sun inclines away and the setting sun passes aside, showing daylight physically redirected rather than spread without obstruction.
The moon follows the sun between the oath to its ḍuḥā and the oath to revealing day; it may support the bright-night branch of the image, though the ayah does not name night or moonlight.
God spreads cloud across the sky before breaking it into fragments and bringing rain; this may invert the dictionary's spreading, cloudless light, though the ayah does not say the cloud dims the sun.
Night جَنَّ عَلَيْهِ, covered Abraham, and he saw a star within it; the scene directly combines an enclosing night with light that remains visible under the cover.
The towns are asked whether punishment might reach them by night while they sleep; it supplies the night-and-repose half of the deliberate pair completed by the forenoon scene in 7:98.
God equally knows one hidden by night and one going openly by day, so nocturnal cover never entails divine absence or concealment from Him.

The Prophet is told to await his Lord's judgment because he is under divine eyes and to glorify on rising; this directly answers apparent silence with watchful care and leads into the night scene of 52:49.
Glorification during the night continues until the stars withdraw, joining a wakeful night to the visible boundary where its cover lifts.
Revelation is sent down during the Night of Decree, making night itself a setting of divine address rather than abandonment or empty silence.
Angels and the Spirit descend in that night by their Lord's permission, giving concrete action and commanded presence within the still night named in 97:1.
Lightning that brings fear and hope appears with heavy clouds, a cloud-borne and unstable brightness that bounds the source dictionary's cloudless light.
The Prophet is commanded to keep an extra vigil during part of the night, a deliberate waking use that marks the boundary of night as ordinary repose.
One who devoutly stands and prostrates through hours of night inhabits the resting time in wakeful worship, while still relying on its distinctive quiet.
The righteous sleep only a little of the night, explicitly reversing the usual repose and continuing toward their dawn practice in 51:18.
The command to stand through the night except a little turns the time of settled rest into sustained recitation, the active boundary already explained by 73:6.
Within the fasting night's own context, spouses are called garments for one another; night and clothing thus meet in an image of mutual nearness, shelter, and concealment.
Abraham next sees the moon rising and then setting, extending 6:76's covered-night scene through the appearance and disappearance of its greater light.
Abraham then sees the sun rising and later setting; this completes the star-moon-sun passage and makes even the largest daylight source subject to arrival and withdrawal.
Created shadows prostrate morning and evening, making their daily change a visible response to the same moving light that extends and retracts cover.
The shadows of created things incline right and left in humble prostration, another concrete formulation of cover changing position under ordered light.
God makes shade, shelters, and garments that protect from heat, supplying protective forms of cover at the bodily boundary of unobstructed sunlight.
The commanded span from the sun's decline through night darkness to dawn recitation lays out the transitions by which daylight closes and reopens.
The Prophet is told to glorify before sunrise and sunset, during night, and at the day's edges so that he may be content, joining the full light-dark cycle to the same addressee's promised رضا.
The question who can guard people by night and day locates protection through both times in the Merciful, making the cycle's security an act of continuing care.
The mountains glorify with David at evening and إِشْرَاق, sunrise brightness, giving the spreading morning hour a responsive created scene.
The clear Book is sent down in a blessed night, a second direct formulation of revelatory presence entering nocturnal stillness.
The Prophet is told to be patient and glorify before sunrise and sunset, placing reassurance and praise at both visible boundaries of the day.
The command continues with glorification during the night, completing 50:39's sunrise-sunset frame with the covered interval itself.
At the approach of dawn the same people seek forgiveness, completing 51:17's wakeful night with an action at the edge where night yields to morning.
The night is better than a thousand months, explicitly denying that darkness or temporal stillness makes the interval empty or deficient.
The new moons are declared time-markers for people, adding another Quranic meeting of nocturnal light with the naming and measuring of time.

Voices are hushed before the Merciful until only a whisper is heard; this may parallel the source's secondary detail of a sound-stilled world, though the ayah's scene is resurrection rather than night.

People cover themselves with their garments to refuse Noah's call; this may illuminate the cloth action behind the source image by reversal, since human covering here shuts out speech rather than sheltering its arrival.
